text: I was going to rip into these guys and say they didn't do their research but the things I am going to point out were not put into play until January of 2023 by Nvidia on GeForce now. But this card is awesome and I bought it over a RTX4080. So if you are old or just too cheap and don't feel like dumping 3000 grand to play Cyberpunk with HDR and Ray tracing enable at 120 FPS you can do it at a fraction of the price on a GTX3050. Even though these guys are crapping all over this card you can buy it for like 170 bucks today and it is the first generation that supports HDMI 2.1 VRR, AV1 and HDR10. So you can buy this card put it on a old pile of crap like my AMD 6300 and play the most killer games on GeForce Now for 19 bucks a month. It would take you over 12 years to spend that on this service which is always being updated versus your 3000 grand computer would be a dumpster fire like mine after 12 years. And better yet go take that 3000 bucks and invest it into a Market SP500 index and make 10-12 percent a year and the interest alone pays for GeForce Now subscription and you'll have extra money left over to compound on that investment. So to me this GPU is awesome. It doesn't have all the games but if you are a casual gamer that has a life, it's a great option.

text:
MSRP is great and all, however: if you pay even $230 for a 1660 Ti today, then you're overpaying. If you buy any 1660 ti that isn't bottom dollar, then your a sucker. If you want to pay a premium to get premium cooling on a legacy card, then you need to get your priorities straight.

Based on what I see: don't pay over 230 for EITHER of these cards, and buy the one that's cheapest. And that will likely be the 1660 ti. THAT card can be had for dirt cheap if ya know how to look and have a little patience.

And don't buy a 3050/2060 on the basis of Ray Tracing! WHY? Because it'll never beat the 1660 ti in performance in tests where its ray tracing is enabled.

In that respect, 3050/2060 barely deserve the RTX label.

But this is merely my opinion. Hehe. Listen to the experts here at LTT.

text:
First, this GPU can't be found right now so no one really knows what it's going to cost.  When the 6500 XT was launched, it was available for a short time at about $300 USD.  But now you can actually get some different models for about $260, AND it's still available.  A point I was challenged on for the 6500 XT review is if the MSRP now reflects that 25% tariff.  Well, if you can now buy a 6500 XT for $260, and a 25% tariff would take a $200 cost up to $250, then apparently the price is baked into the MSRP.  Why?  Answer follows.

Global inflation is adding 15 - 20% to production costs.  Then, EU countries have a 20 - 25% VAT on certain imports, and GPUs from China, where over 90% of ALL GPUs come from fall into that list.  And then the US added a 25% tariff on many products coming out of China, and this also affects Canada as Linus discussed back in Feb 2021 on a video from LTT.  This tariff went into effect Jan 1, 2021, so it makes the cost of a new GPU ridiculous, and a budget GPU is now a bad buy.  Really bad. If you don't have the money to buy a high quality GPU and pay the insane price, and you need to buy a budget GPU, you're better off getting an APU.  Sorry, new world unless you want the stripped down 6500 XT.  Once again there are no RTX 3050s to be found.  I doubt you'll be able to find one for less than $350 USD.

AMD has succeeded in putting out something scalpers are hesitant to buy up.  This GPU?  It's going to be a BIG target.  I doubt the 6500 XT will come down below $250 USD because of added costs as discussed below.  The RTX 3050?  Good luck finding one.  Scalpers have sold about 50,000 Nvidia 3000 series GPUs through ebay and StockX already, and because this is a low cost GPU, it will be targeted like crazy, just like other low cost PC parts have been.

https://www.pcmag.com/news/scalpers-have-sold-50000-nvidia-rtx-3000-gpus-through-ebay-stockx


Yes Anthony, almost all GPUs come out of China.  The other place they come out of is Taiwan, but it's a small percentage.  Nvidia even talked about this in an appeal to Biden to drop tariffs on GPUs, and those tariffs ARE baked into the MSRP.  They have to be now.  If they weren't you'd see too much of a price difference for NEW products.  In fact this product proves that 25% tariff is baked into the MSRP:

https://www.newegg.com/asus-radeon-rx-6500-xt-dual-rx6500xt-o4g/p/N82E16814126553?Description=6500%20XT&cm_re=6500_XT--14-126-553--Product

And, ASUS GPUs come out of China.  So if it's right at MSRP it probably means they've been able to produce it for a low cost and they're selling it for under MSRP, but after price increases elsewhere in the supply chains, it's back at $200 USD as discussed below.

The tariffs weren't baked in to MSRP back in 2020, because the tariff in the US wasn't in effect at that time.  It had gone into place, but was held off by Trump, and I assume it's because he didn't want to lose the 2020 election because EVERYONE being mad at him for so much inflation?  Instead he delayed it to after the election, Jan 1, 2021, and Biden decided to keep them in place so HE could be blamed for all the inflation, because he's an idiot.  

https://gizmodo.com/nvidia-asks-biden-admin-to-exempt-graphics-cards-from-t-1848158150

https://www.pcmag.com/news/will-the-tariffs-on-graphics-cards-lift-soon-eh-it-may-be-a-while

https://www.pcmag.com/news/prices-for-graphics-cards-and-motherboards-go-up-as-us-tariffs-kick-back


And why is pricing still a bit over MSRP?  Not because of the 25% tariff which is already baked into the MSRP.  It's because EVERY point in the supply chain, shipping from China, getting GPUs to suppliers and retailers because of how much more truckers have to be paid because the US is short about 40,000 truckers, and retailers are paying 25 - 50% more for their employees.  You also have the issue where different makers of GPUs have different costs, and probably most have more costs than what AMD goes by in setting it's MSRP.  For sure premium GPUs such as PowerColor are going to cost more, by a bit.

https://www.cnn.com/2021/05/29/economy/truck-driver-shortage-pay-hikes/index.html

https://www.businessinsider.com/trucking-shortage-transportation-inflation-high-transportation-costs-through-year-2021-5#:~:text=A%20shortage%20of%20semi-conductors%20to%20build%20new%20trucks,and%20houses%20have%20all%20become%20more%20expensive%20lately.

https://sharerig.com/blog/the-trucking-industry-faces-massive-shortages-of-drivers-in-2022

https://www.cnbc.com/2021/11/19/surging-shipping-costs-to-drive-consumer-price-inflation-unctad-says.html


Amazon is paying 50% more than before Covid started, going from about $12/hr to $18/hr for warehouse workers as an example, and newegg and EVERY brick and mortar retailer in the US that's going to carry computer parts is dealing with higher wages.  

https://qz.com/2060508/what-amazons-18-average-hourly-wage-means-for-other-employers/#:~:text=Amazon%20is%20raising%20its%20average%20hourly%20US%20wage,increased%20demand%20for%20online%20goods%2C%20fueling%20Amazon%E2%80%99s%20business.


So every point in the journey of getting a GPU from China to the consumer costs more, and companies have to make a profit, and don't want to accept smaller margins.  So all the companies along the supply chain including the retailers are taking more money, and it's bringing the price up quite a bit from MSRP.  That's why a $200 MSRP GPU is selling for $260.  Some of these companies are certainly charging more than they should, but to be fair the market is so unstable that these companies are trying to figure out what their new costs should be.  This markup is going to affect the low cost items more than an expensive product, especially on shipping where shipping an expensive GPU isn't much different than shipping a cheap GPU.

text: I'd say the RTX 3050 was launched as a response to AMD's 6500xt and had to be done so fast obviously. text:
My disappointment comes from realizing the fact, that the newer gpu models hardly surpass previous generations. The processing nodes are smaller, thus actually enabling higher efficiency i.e. more performance per watt. But instead we see top tier GPUs with even more electric power hunger. The same goes for dead baked, upheated x86 cpus. This is insane.

I wished, we gamers had something similar like apple's efficient M1 but open source based with a similar Rosetta 2 compatibility layer for x86 legacy. This is, what i would actually like to see in the next versions of the steam deck. 

If we embraced something similar like floss in Gnu Linux but for chips, we were no slaves to serve three main corporations anymore, who divide up the market among each other and artificially keep chip prices high by keeping the chip outputs to low contingents. They could have served gamers with affordable formidable mid tier gpus since a long time already. But instead they preferred to sell attractive chips to miners first for years. And what they do offer us now, is, expressed in mild words ... suboptimal.

1070 here and I have no idea what I can expect from a GPU upgrade.

now if you want even better, you got the Radeon RX 6800 and RTX 3080, those two would be worth the upgrade, but the only thing you'd have to worry about is power consumption especially if you get the 3080.

text:
i would think so, of course you can always go on PC Partpicker and lay out a build and they'll give you an estimated wattage. but that would include everything in your PC currently. on PC Partpicker you'll have to map out your exact build, and then switch a few things around you don't have.

CPU
CPU Cooler
motherboard
Ram
Storage
GPU

those are just a few things, usually what i do is look on the back and see what the graphics card recommends. it's not a complete accurate description since they could be basing it on what CPU, Ram, and motherboard you might have, but they try to go by the biggest power draw you might get when combining this card. with the 3080 your looking at roughly 300 watts, but when you add the 12700K that's another 125 watt at it's default, but we know it can go higher.
so a 1000 watt would probably be what you'd need, but i would make sure it's a good brand and is 80 plus gold.

text:
I feel like this will be a fantastic value card for the money... on the used market in 3 years.

EDIT June 2025: Might as well follow this up since people keep commenting 3 years later, usually telling me how wrong I was, lmao. *TL;DR*, probably buy a used GTX 1080 instead, but if driver support for the foreseeable future is a non-negotiable then it's a good card for less than $100. Ebay auctions are the main way to get a 3050 8GB sub-$100; don't bother with Buy-It-Now listings as they are usually $130+.

For most gaming a used GTX 1080 is a much better value at $100, though. In many games released AFTER the 3050 launched, the 1080 loses the lead but not by an unplayable margin, usually like 5 - 15 fps. (That trend will probably continue and become more noticeable as Pascal continues to age, because even fine wine goes bad at some point.) The 1080 will probably stomp the 3050 in any game released pre-2020, though. 

Saving up an extra $50 - $75 gives you many other options, though, if the idea of drivers ending circa 2027 is emotionally distressing to you. A 2060 Super, an RX 5700, or an RX 6600 all will regularly fall in that $150 - $175 range. If you're lucky, you might even nab a 6600 XT or 6650 XT in that range through an auction. 

But seriously, if you don't care about driver support probably ending within the next two or three years, a GTX 1080 beats a 3050 at the $100 price point and you can easily get one at that price without an auction. Really the only liability there is if a major Pascal security hole is found after support ends.

IMO, post-covid 10 series prices are lower now than they otherwise would be had they not commanded such high prices during COVID. Once supply of newer cards caught up to demand towards the end of COVID, Pascal card prices dropped off a cliff. In a world where the 10 series' relevancy to non-budget customers tapered off rather than spiking and then falling off, a used 3050 8GB would probably be a better value proposition outside of auction listings. As it is, buy a 1080.

text: @lizexi7115  Supply chain is being disrupted in large part due to Taiwan and China. One of the biggest chip manufacturers in the world is Taiwan Semi Conductors, or TSMC. They make chips for everyone from AMD, Nvidia, Samsung, Sony etc. They are located, as their name suggests, in Taiwan. If the Chinese-Taiwan relationship continues to deteriorate, China could very well blockade or even invade the island entirely. They have been conducting military exercises in the area for months now. As such, many customers of TSMC are worried and looking for alternative companies to make chips in case the worst happens. Keep in mind chipsets are typically ordered years in advance, so if TSMC goes down companies would be down YEARS worth of stock they can't replace. This is stressing other manufactorers that cannot pick up the slack immediately. Thus the problem continues. I'm not saying its the only factor, but it's a major factor.

text:
@lordv1le859  What are you basing this on? 

FSR relies on spatial upscaling, which is a much more basic than DLSS and Intel's XeSS. It can improve but its limited by its technology, and AMD has also abandoned in favour of RSR.

Don't get me wrong, not shitting on AMD here at all, rather FSR. RSR will be much more competitive. 

RSR will still have the drawbacks of a lower tech approach, but implementation (across all games rather than relying on developer implementation) gives it significant advantages over Nvidia. 

However, RSR will be exclusive to AMD's latest cards, which means that older Nvidia card's won't benefit from it.
author: @JimIBobIJones

text:
@lordv1le859  Look it up. Its a different technology completely. DLSS and Intel's XeSS relies on supersampling, which is objectively superior to spatial upscaling. 

FSR is based on traditional, spatial upscaling and sharpening.

text:
@first last Similar thoughts here. People with high expectations, who bought a PS5 and tasted next gen graphics by demos like Matrix Awakened, may complain from that on about outdated cross gen fall back compatibility graphics. The latter ones are actually to support widespread old PS4, xbox consoles and pc gpus like mainstream gtx 1060 and rx 570 etc. But they draw back the possible max visuals of next gen. That's why most ray tracing titles are almost indistinguishable, when their features are shut off to fall back mode.
Games Consoles got the biggest market share. So especially small but often amazing game studios may have to calculate, if they could afford the extra development costs any longer at some point. The old rasterization method of computer graphics needs much more work for example baked in lightmaps, while ray tracing doesn't need that. Models don't need time consuming LoD substeps on new hardware anymore. The list goes on.
Some people hope, that intel may change something, but their gpus might not reach too many gamers, due to the promised specs, which attracts miners. I doubt intel's drivers to be that ripe and flawless for games anyway. Their UHD drivers suck in games. But either way in regard of gaming performance, intel very probably is going to earn money.
Actually, also big console gaming became an expensive hobby.

Among the few viable options i see, is the steam deck, which might come to the rescue of many gamers.

In 1902 the German Empire introduced a tax on sparkling wine, initially meant to finance his majesty's, Kaiser Wilhelms, navy. The Kaiser and his navy are long gone and Germany is a republic now, but guess what remained until today, raking in about half a billion dollars annually...

A tax once introduce will never go away! That's why I'm afraid the "RTX-tax", the "mining-tax" and the "supply-shortage-tax" are also here to stay even after all of those issues are resolved. Nvidia and AMD tasted the sweet blood of price gouging, now they won't easily part from their huge profit margins - unless Intel can actually do something about it. We can only hope!

text: @nicoj9984  This will be/should be solved by supply and demand. If chip manufacturers can make more GPU's in the near future, at a certain point there will be more graphics cards than people want to buy (at that inflated price) so prices will HAVE to go down. As there are (soon) 3 players in that market, it only takes one of them to lower their prices and the others have to follow. Borderlands - 8 gb

Its all well and good pushing the boundaries of graphics and the like, but I don't need all the 4k crazy textures realistic textures. text: While the 6500xt is an objectively bad card, the price is right in line with where it should be, at least at MSRP.  Between inflation and the GPU tariff $200 today only buys you $150 worth of GPU at 2017 prices.  Which slots it in $20 below an rx570 at launch price adjusted to 2017. The same is true with the RTX 3050, $250 worth of GPU today only buys you $175 worth of 2017 GPU.  While the shortages and supply issues have well covered reasons, I'm surprised none of the tech coverage has given much thought to the fact that the US dollar buys a lot less today than it did 5 years ago, or the larger issue that consumers in the US are paying 25% more than they used to with no benefit due to an idiotic tariff.
